cards.title: Disasters and Multiple Sites: Two Special Rules
cards.content:
This lesson covers the last two general guidelines in Section I.B:

• **Section I.B.19 — Coding for healthcare encounters in hurricane aftermath.** After a hurricane, many patients are treated for injuries and for problems caused by losing their homes, power, or access to care. This guideline explains how to use **external cause of morbidity codes** and **Z codes** so the data about the disaster is complete and accurate.
• **Section I.B.20 — Multiple sites coding.** What "multiple" means in ICD-10-CM and when to code each site separately versus using a "multiple sites" code.

The hurricane guideline is also a good review of how external cause codes work in general: they **explain** an injury, they are **never** the principal or first-listed diagnosis, and they are sequenced **after** the injury code.

boxes.b: When to use external cause codes
Sequencing: hurricane first among external causes
Injuries not caused directly by the storm
Z codes for social and access issues

cards.title: In Plain English: External Cause Codes After a Hurricane
cards.content:
An **external cause of morbidity code** explains **how** an injury or health condition happened. Section I.B.19.a says one should be assigned to identify the cause of injuries incurred as a result of the hurricane.

What external cause codes capture (per the guideline):

• **Cause** — how the injury or health condition happened
• **Intent** — unintentional/accidental, or intentional (such as suicide or assault)
• **Place** where the event occurred
• **Activity** of the patient at the time of the event
• **Status** of the person (e.g., civilian, military)

These codes are **supplemental** — they add to the ICD-10-CM codes that describe the injury itself.

cards.title: The Sequencing and Setting Rules in I.B.19.a
cards.content:
Section I.B.19.a also sets firm rules on placement and use:

• **Never principal or first-listed.** External cause codes are never recorded as a principal diagnosis (first-listed in non-inpatient settings).
• **Injury code first.** The appropriate injury code is sequenced **before** any external cause codes.
• **Injury, adverse effect or poisoning required.** Do **not** assign external cause codes for encounters to treat hurricane victims' medical conditions when **no injury, adverse effect or poisoning** is involved.
• **Every encounter.** Assign external cause codes for **each encounter** for care and treatment of the injury.
• **All settings.** External cause codes may be assigned in all health care settings.
• **Broad definition of setting.** After the hurricane, a healthcare setting is **any location where medical care is provided by licensed healthcare professionals**.

**Exam trap:** A hurricane victim treated for a medical condition with no injury, adverse effect or poisoning does **not** get an external cause code just because the hurricane happened.

cards.title: Worked Example: Treated at a Shelter
cards.content:
**Documentation:** After a hurricane, a licensed nurse practitioner treats a patient for a laceration at an emergency shelter. The patient was cut by debris during the storm. The patient returns two days later for wound care.

**Which guideline applies?** Section I.B.19.a.

**Decision:**

• The shelter **counts as a healthcare setting** — care was provided by a licensed healthcare professional.
• Sequence the **injury (laceration) code first**, then the external cause code(s).
• Assign the external cause code(s) at the **first visit and again at the follow-up visit**, since both are encounters for care and treatment of the injury.

**Variation:** If another evacuee at the shelter is seen only for a medical condition with **no injury, adverse effect or poisoning**, no external cause code is assigned.

cards.question: According to Section I.B.19.a, where are external cause of morbidity codes sequenced for a hurricane-related injury?
options: After the appropriate injury code
As the principal diagnosis, because they explain the reason for the visit
Only on the first encounter for the injury
They are not used in non-inpatient settings
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.19.a states that external cause codes are never recorded as a principal diagnosis (first-listed in non-inpatient settings) and that the appropriate injury code should be sequenced before any external cause codes. Option B contradicts that. Option C is wrong because external cause codes should be assigned for each encounter for care and treatment of the injury. Option D is wrong because they may be assigned in all health care settings.

visual.hint: Which comes first: what the injury is, or how it happened?

cards.question: After a hurricane, a patient comes to a clinic for a refill of a regular medication for a chronic medical condition. There is no injury, adverse effect or poisoning. What does Section I.B.19.a say about external cause codes?
options: Assign the hurricane external cause code as the first-listed code
Assign the hurricane external cause code as a secondary code
Do not assign external cause codes for this encounter
Assign external cause codes only if the clinic is a hospital
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.19.a says external cause codes should not be assigned for encounters to treat hurricane victims' medical conditions when no injury, adverse effect or poisoning is involved. Options A and B assign codes the guideline says not to use (and A also violates the never-first-listed rule). Option D is wrong because setting is not the issue; external cause codes may be assigned in all health care settings when they apply.

visual.hint: Is there an injury, adverse effect or poisoning?

cards.title: In Plain English: The Hurricane Code Goes First Among External Causes
cards.content:
Section I.B.19.b explains how to order external cause codes when there is more than one.

**Priority rule:** codes for **cataclysmic events**, such as a hurricane, take priority over **all other external cause codes except child and adult abuse and terrorism**, and are sequenced before other external cause of injury codes.

**Use as many as needed:** assign as many external cause codes as necessary to fully explain each cause.

**The guideline's example:** an injury from a **building collapse during the hurricane** gets external cause codes for **both** the hurricane and the building collapse, with the **hurricane** code sequenced as the **first external cause code**.

**Full order for an injury directly caused by the hurricane:**
1. Code(s) for the **injuries**
2. **X37.0-, Hurricane** (with the appropriate 7th character)
3. Any other applicable external cause of injury codes

boxes.b: First external cause code, with 7th character

cards.title: Flood, Levee, or Dam? Choosing the Right Code
cards.content:
The rest of I.B.19.b separates causes that are easy to mix up:

• **Flooding from a levee breaking related to the hurricane:** code **X37.0-** also should be assigned.
• **Flooding resulting directly from the storm:** assign **X38.-, Flood** (with the appropriate 7th character).
• **Collapse caused by the hurricane:** do **not** assign **X36.0-, Collapse of dam or man-made structure**.
• **X36.0- is limited** to collapses of man-made structures due to **earth surface movements**, not due to storm surges directly from a hurricane.

**Exam trap:** A structure that collapses because of the hurricane is **not** coded with X36.0-. That code is only for collapses from earth surface movements.

Note: the official text prints this code once as "X36.0.-" and once as "X36.0-"; both refer to the same code, Collapse of dam or man-made structure.

cards.title: Worked Example: Injured When a Building Collapsed
cards.content:
**Documentation:** A patient has a fractured arm after the roof of a store collapsed on them during a hurricane.

**Which guideline applies?** Section I.B.19.b (this mirrors the guideline's building-collapse example).

**Decision:**

1. Sequence the **fracture** (the injury) first.
2. Assign **X37.0-, Hurricane**, with the appropriate 7th character, as the **first external cause code**.
3. Add an external cause code for the **building collapse**, since the guideline says to assign codes for both the hurricane and the building collapse.

**What not to do:** Do **not** use **X36.0-, Collapse of dam or man-made structure**, because the collapse was due to the hurricane. X36.0- is limited to collapses from earth surface movements.

cards.question: A patient is injured when a structure collapses during a hurricane. Which statement follows Section I.B.19.b?
options: Assign X36.0-, Collapse of dam or man-made structure, as the first external cause code
Assign the external cause codes first, followed by the injury code
Assign only the hurricane code, because only one external cause code is allowed
Assign external cause codes for both the hurricane and the building collapse, with X37.0-, Hurricane, as the first external cause code
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.19.b says that for an injury from a building collapse during the hurricane, external cause codes for both the hurricane and the building collapse should be assigned, with the hurricane code as the first external cause code. Option A is wrong because X36.0- should not be assigned when the collapse is due to the hurricane. Option C is wrong because you assign as many external cause codes as necessary to fully explain each cause. Option B is wrong because the injury code is sequenced before external cause codes (I.B.19.a).

visual.hint: How many external cause codes may be used, and which goes first?

cards.question: Under Section I.B.19.b, codes for cataclysmic events such as a hurricane take priority over all other external cause codes EXCEPT:
options: Codes for place of occurrence and activity
Codes for child and adult abuse and terrorism
Codes for transport accidents
Codes for flood
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.19.b states that codes for cataclysmic events take priority over all other external cause codes except child and adult abuse and terrorism. Options A, C and D are not named as exceptions, so the hurricane code is sequenced before them.

visual.hint: Two exceptions are named in the guideline.

cards.question: A patient is injured by floodwater that came from a levee breaking because of a hurricane. According to Section I.B.19.b, which code also should be assigned?
options: X37.0-, Hurricane
X36.0-, Collapse of dam or man-made structure
No external cause code, because the levee failed, not the storm
Z59.1, Inadequate housing, as the first-listed code
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.19.b states that code X37.0- also should be assigned when an injury is incurred as a result of flooding caused by a levee breaking related to the hurricane. Option B is wrong because X36.0- is limited to collapses due to earth surface movements, not storm surges from a hurricane. Option C contradicts the guideline. Option D is not supported; nothing in the scenario documents inadequate housing, and the injury code comes first.

visual.hint: The guideline addresses this exact situation.

cards.title: In Plain English: Was the Injury a Direct Result of the Hurricane?
cards.content:
Section I.B.19.c deals with injuries that happen **during the hurricane period but not because of the storm**.

• **Not a direct result:** for example, an **evacuee** injured in a **motor vehicle accident**. Assign the external cause code(s) that describe the actual cause, but **do not** assign **X37.0-, Hurricane**.
• **Not clear whether it was a direct result:** **assume the injury is due to the hurricane**. Assign **X37.0-, Hurricane**, plus any other applicable external cause codes.

Other external cause codes the guideline names as possibly applicable, in addition to X37.0-:

• **X30-, Exposure to excessive natural heat**
• **X31-, Exposure to excessive natural cold**
• **X38-, Flood**

**Exam trap:** The default when it is **unclear** is to **assume** the hurricane caused it — this is the opposite of what many students guess.

boxes.b: Code the real cause; no X37.0-
X30- heat, X31- cold, X38- flood

cards.question: An evacuee is injured in a motor vehicle accident while driving away from the hurricane area. The injury was not a direct result of the hurricane. According to Section I.B.19.c, what should the coder do?
options: Assign X37.0-, Hurricane, as the first external cause code
Assign no external cause codes
Assign external cause code(s) describing the cause of the injury, but not X37.0-, Hurricane
Assume the hurricane caused the injury
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.19.c uses this example: for an evacuee injured in a motor vehicle accident, assign the appropriate external cause code(s) to describe the cause of the injury, but do not assign code X37.0-, Hurricane. Option A assigns the hurricane code the guideline excludes. Option B is wrong because the injury still needs external cause codes for its actual cause. Option D applies only when it is not clear whether the injury was a direct result of the hurricane.

visual.hint: Was the hurricane the direct cause here?

cards.question: The record does not make clear whether a patient's injury was a direct result of a hurricane. What does Section I.B.19.c instruct?
options: Query the provider and hold the claim
Do not assign any external cause code
Assign X36.0-, Collapse of dam or man-made structure
Assume the injury is due to the hurricane and assign X37.0-, Hurricane, plus any other applicable external cause codes
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.19.c states, "If it is not clear whether the injury was a direct result of the hurricane, assume the injury is due to the hurricane and assign code X37.0-, Hurricane, as well as any other applicable external cause of morbidity codes." Option A is not what this guideline instructs; it gives a default instead. Option B ignores the instruction. Option C is wrong because X36.0- is limited to collapses from earth surface movements and has nothing to do with this scenario.

visual.hint: This guideline gives a default assumption.

cards.title: In Plain English: Z Codes After a Hurricane
cards.content:
**Z codes** describe **other reasons for healthcare encounters**. Section I.B.19.d says they may be assigned to:

• further explain the reasons for presenting for healthcare services, **including transfers between healthcare facilities**, or
• provide **additional information** relevant to the encounter.

The Official Guidelines identify which Z codes may be **principal/first-listed only**, **secondary only**, or **either**, depending on the circumstances.

Possible applicable Z codes listed in the guideline:

• **Z59.0-**, Homelessness
• **Z59.1**, Inadequate housing
• **Z59.5**, Extreme poverty
• **Z75.1**, Person awaiting admission to adequate facility elsewhere
• **Z75.3**, Unavailability and inaccessibility of health-care facilities
• **Z75.4**, Unavailability and inaccessibility of other helping agencies
• **Z76.2**, Encounter for health supervision and care of other healthy infant and child
• **Z99.12**, Encounter for respirator [ventilator] dependence during power failure

cards.title: Not an All-Inclusive List
cards.content:
The last paragraph of I.B.19.d gives three practical instructions:

• **The lists are examples.** The external cause codes and Z codes listed are **not all-inclusive**. Other codes may apply based on the documentation.
• **Code completely.** Assign **as many codes as necessary** to fully explain each healthcare encounter.
• **Use what you have.** Because patient history may be **very limited** after a disaster, use **any available documentation** to assign the appropriate external cause and Z codes.

**What it does NOT mean:** It does not mean you may guess at codes without documentation. The codes must still be based on the documentation that is available.

cards.title: Worked Example: Ventilator and a Power Outage
cards.content:
**Documentation:** After a hurricane knocks out electricity, a patient who depends on a home ventilator comes to a hospital because the ventilator has no power. The patient's home was also destroyed, and the provider documents that the patient is now homeless.

**Which guideline applies?** Section I.B.19.d.

**Decision:**

• **Z99.12**, Encounter for respirator [ventilator] dependence during power failure, explains the reason for the encounter.
• **Z59.0-**, Homelessness, adds relevant information (completed to the full code the documentation supports).
• Assign as many codes as necessary to fully explain the encounter.
• Check the Official Guidelines for whether each Z code may be first-listed, secondary only, or either.

**No external cause code is needed** for the power-failure visit itself if no injury, adverse effect or poisoning is involved (I.B.19.a).

cards.question: Which statement about the Z codes listed in Section I.B.19.d is correct?
options: Only the Z codes listed may be used for hurricane-related encounters
The list is not all-inclusive; other codes may apply based on the documentation
Z codes may never be used for transfers between healthcare facilities
Only one Z code may be assigned per encounter
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.19.d states that the external cause codes and Z codes listed are not an all-inclusive list and that other codes may be applicable based upon the documentation. Option A contradicts this. Option C is wrong because the guideline specifically mentions transfers between healthcare facilities. Option D is wrong because the guideline says to assign as many codes as necessary to fully explain each encounter.

visual.hint: Is the list a complete list or a set of examples?

cards.title: In Plain English: Multiple Sites
cards.content:
Section I.B.20 defines **"multiple"** in ICD-10-CM as involving **two or more sites**.

The decision order:

1. **Chapter-specific guidelines come first.** Follow them when they address "multiple sites."
2. **No chapter-specific guideline and the sites are specified:** assign codes describing the **specified sites individually**.
3. **Sites not documented:** assign the appropriate code for **"multiple sites."**

**What it does NOT mean:** a "multiple sites" code is not a shortcut when the record names each site. If the specified sites are documented, code them individually (unless a chapter-specific guideline says otherwise).

cards.title: Worked Example: Two Joints Named, or Not Named
cards.content:
**Scenario 1:** The provider documents a condition affecting two specific, named joints. No chapter-specific guideline addresses multiple sites for this condition.

**Decision:** Under Section I.B.20, assign codes describing **each specified site individually**.

**Scenario 2:** The provider documents the same type of condition affecting "multiple sites" but never says which ones.

**Decision:** The specified sites are **not documented**, so assign the appropriate code for **"multiple sites."**

**Exam trap:** The word "multiple" in the record does not automatically mean the "multiple sites" code. Check first whether the sites are named.

cards.question: A provider documents a condition affecting two specified sites, and there is no chapter-specific guideline for multiple sites. According to Section I.B.20, how should it be coded?
options: Assign codes describing the specified sites individually
Assign the code for "multiple sites"
Assign the code for the more severe site only
Assign an unspecified site code
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.20 states that in the absence of chapter-specific guidelines, assign codes describing specified sites individually when documented. Option B applies only when the specified sites are not documented. Options C and D are not supported by the guideline; the sites are known and both should be reported.

cards.title: Applying I.B.19 and I.B.20 on a Real Record
cards.content:
**For a hurricane-related encounter:**

1. **Is there an injury, adverse effect or poisoning?** If not, do not assign external cause codes (I.B.19.a). Consider Z codes instead (I.B.19.d).
2. **Sequence the injury code(s) first.** External cause codes are never principal or first-listed (I.B.19.a).
3. **Was the injury a direct result of the hurricane?**
   • Yes, or unclear: assign **X37.0-, Hurricane**, as the first external cause code (I.B.19.b, I.B.19.c).
   • No (e.g., an evacuee's car accident): code the actual cause; do not assign X37.0- (I.B.19.c).
4. **Add other external causes** as needed — for example, the building collapse, X38.- for flooding directly from the storm, X30- or X31- for heat or cold exposure. Do not use X36.0- for a collapse caused by the hurricane (I.B.19.b, I.B.19.c).
5. **Repeat external cause codes** at each encounter for the injury (I.B.19.a).
6. **Add Z codes** for homelessness, housing, access to care, transfers, or power failure as documented (I.B.19.d).

**For any record that mentions multiple sites:**

7. Check chapter-specific guidelines; code named sites individually; use "multiple sites" only when the sites are not documented (I.B.20).

boxes.b: No: skip X37.0-; unclear: use it

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.content:
• External cause codes after a hurricane explain **cause, intent, place, activity and status**; they are **supplemental** and **never principal or first-listed** (I.B.19.a).
• The **injury code comes first**; external cause codes follow and are assigned at **each encounter** for the injury (I.B.19.a).
• **No injury, adverse effect or poisoning = no external cause code** for a hurricane victim's medical condition (I.B.19.a).
• A healthcare setting is **any location where licensed healthcare professionals provide care** (I.B.19.a).
• Cataclysmic event codes like **X37.0-, Hurricane**, come first among external causes, **except** child and adult abuse and terrorism (I.B.19.b).
• **Not** X36.0- for a collapse due to the hurricane; **X37.0-** for levee-break flooding related to the hurricane; **X38.-** for flooding directly from the storm (I.B.19.b).
• Indirect injury: no X37.0-. **Unclear: assume the hurricane** (I.B.19.c).
• Z code lists are examples; use any available documentation (I.B.19.d). "Multiple" means **two or more sites**; code named sites individually (I.B.20).

cards.question: Which statement about external cause codes in hurricane aftermath is correct under Section I.B.19.a?
options: They are assigned only at the first encounter for an injury
They may be reported as the first-listed diagnosis in outpatient settings
A healthcare setting is any location where medical care is provided by licensed healthcare professionals
They are required for every hurricane victim, even when no injury, adverse effect or poisoning is involved
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.19.a states that for the purpose of capturing complete and accurate data after the hurricane, a healthcare setting should be considered as any location where medical care is provided by licensed healthcare professionals. Option A is wrong because they should be assigned for each encounter for care and treatment of the injury. Option B is wrong because they are never recorded as principal (first-listed in non-inpatient settings). Option D is wrong because they should not be assigned when no injury, adverse effect or poisoning is involved.

visual.hint: Review the definition of a healthcare setting in the aftermath.

cards.question: A patient is injured by flooding that resulted directly from the hurricane's storm. Based on Section I.B.19.b, which external cause code describes the flooding?
options: X36.0-, Collapse of dam or man-made structure
Z59.1, Inadequate housing
X31-, Exposure to excessive natural cold
X38.-, Flood, with the appropriate 7th character
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.B.19.b states that code X38.-, Flood (with the appropriate 7th character), should be assigned when an injury is from flooding resulting directly from the storm. Option A is limited to collapses of man-made structures due to earth surface movements. Option C describes exposure to cold, not flooding. Option B is a Z code for a social circumstance, not an external cause of injury.

visual.hint: Match the cause named in the scenario to the code title.
